name: Bianca Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of six mortgage processors in the back office of a regional bank. We check the papers for every mortgage application: payslips, bank statements, valuations, ID, all of it, before the underwriters decide. I start at half eight with the queue, hand out cases, check the tricky ones myself and sign off what my team has done. I've only been a team leader since spring, and I'm still slower at it than the woman who had the job before me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's going on in your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting married next August, to Daniel, he's a police officer. I still live with my parents, which some people find odd at 27, but it's how my family does things and it means I've saved a lot for our first house. On Sundays I sing in the church choir. I don't use the AI tools the bank keeps offering, I'd rather read a payslip myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always get excited about new things, and then you still need someone careful to check a mortgage file. At work I'd just say let's get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. A bank is a careful place, and the regulators like a person to have checked the papers. If the AI sorts a few documents into folders, fine, my team still does the real checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep learning the team leader job, get married as planned, and keep saving for the house. I'd not touch the AI unless my manager told me I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your plans with Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. My parents have a spare room for as long as we need it, so we're not in a rush. In a world where AI is mostly hype, I get married in August, we buy a house near my parents, and I keep checking mortgages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your Sunday look like a year from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make him come on Sundays, I think, that's the deal. Daniel's not as churchy as me, but he knows how much it matters.

At work I'd just say **get on with it**.

do: Keep learning the **team leader** job at her own pace.

Avoid the **AI tools** unless her manager insists.

fieldNote: Her security rests on **savings**, low costs at home and trust in banking rules.

steps.text: Keep checking mortgage files by hand with the team
Marry Daniel next August as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, and that the bank shouldn't throw away people who've done good work for years. I'd say it nicely, I'm not one for protests. I'd talk about it more at home than at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, checking payslips and bank statements is exactly the sort of thing on that list. I think my team goes from six to two or three, and they'd want a team leader who's good with the system. That's not me, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare bit of money even harder, maybe push the house purchase back a year. I'd ask about moving to a mortgage adviser job in a branch, where you sit with the couple in front of you. People want a face when they borrow that much money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd mean that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents' spare room keeps coming up. What does it mean to you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful, that's what I'd feel. Living with my parents at 27 looked old-fashioned to my friends, but in a world like that it would be the smartest money decision I ever made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel say about all of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we'll be fine, and I'd believe him. Police work isn't going to a computer any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and families will have to stick together. I'd say the government should help people find real work, not just hand out money. And I'd say it at church, where people actually look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the whole back office is gone by 2028, me included. Even the branch adviser job, because a computer can talk you through a mortgage. Daniel's job is safer, at least until the robots, and maybe longer, because people want a real police officer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller and keep the money for the house deposit. I'd cut everything else, the new car, the honeymoon in Greece, all of it. And I'd ask my uncle about his bakery, because I'd rather work with my hands for family than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed, but she'd understand. My mum has been planning my wedding since I was seven, and I'd have to tell my mum it's a church hall and sandwiches now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the bakery give you that the bank doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something real, at least. Bread doesn't come from an app, not for a few years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so there's no need to panic, and young people should learn trades. That's what I'd tell my younger cousins. At work I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have four or so years in the bank and then I'd be done. But it lines up with what I wanted anyway: Daniel and I want children by 30, and I always pictured staying home for a few years. So for me it's less of a shock than it would be for some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving for three or four years, and we'd buy a small house with a big deposit so the mortgage is low. I'd plan for the first baby around 29 and not go back to the bank. I'd lean on Daniel's pay and my savings, and maybe help at my uncle's bakery part time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because one wage is tight. But less frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Daniel's job changes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about that. If my husband's police wage has to carry us, I want a house we could pay off on one salary, not two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be worried about him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope he'd be all right, but I'd be lying if I said I knew. That's why the low mortgage matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will adapt, like they always have. I'd say parents should guide their kids towards solid trades. That's my honest view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly safe. In ten years I'd probably be at home with small children anyway, and Daniel would be a sergeant. The bank job matters less to me than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the bank, maybe get better at leading the team, and still avoid the AI. We'd marry, buy the house, have our children. I'd wait and see what the world looks like before deciding about going back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry, at the back of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd think about. I'd want my children to learn a trade with their hands, because a trade is something no computer can take from them, at least not quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If everything goes as planned, how does your life look at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Faith, family, a house we own. The job was always just the job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as Daniel and I are starting out, before we've got the house. What would help is the government getting people into real jobs and apprenticeships, not just sending money, and banks giving loyal staff time to move. I don't want a handout, I want a job where I can still look someone in the eye at the end of the day.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much faith matters. People at church would look after each other in the hard ones, and I think that counts for more than any plan.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a job where I can still look someone in the eye at the end of the day.
portrait: Bianca is **27** and leads six mortgage processors in a regional bank's back office.
She lives with her parents to save, is **marrying Daniel**, a police officer, next August, and sings in the church choir.
She never uses AI and trusts **careful human checking**.
As AGI nears she leans on **family**, a low mortgage and plans to stay home with children.
She wants **real jobs and trades**, not handouts, for people who lose work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting before she and Daniel have the **house**.
whatWouldHelp: Government help into **real jobs** and apprenticeships, not just money.
